articles.title: Arizona’s lifeline for chip manufacturing is drying up
articles.summary: America’s epicenter for chip manufacturing has to figure out how to cope with far less water from the Colorado River.
articles.body: Arizona, an epicenter for the bipartisan push to revive American chip manufacturing, is about to lose more than a quarter of the water it typically pulls each year from the Colorado River. The 1,400-mile waterway is a crucial lifeline for the region and other western states. A recent federal decision on how to manage its dwindling flow hits Arizona, and its already drought-prone desert communities, particularly hard. The river provides more than a third of the Grand Canyon State’s water. Arizona has been a manufacturing hub since the start of the semiconductor industry, and now it’s where TSMC and Intel are expanding massive factories to make advanced chips for AI — a water-intensive effort. City planners and industry leaders have already taken precautions to conserve water and find alternative sources. It’s a resource that is likely to become more expensive for manufacturers and residents alike as they learn to rely less on the Colorado River. That’s already raising tensions over who shoulders the costs for new infrastructure needed to adapt, as well as what constitutes a good use of water. The challenges that come with managing a limited water supply are only going to grow as AI demands a larger share. “Our economy is changing, and that’s really painful,” says Kathryn Sorensen, research director at the Kyl Center for Water Policy at Arizona State University. “When there’s a water scarcity issue you have to start looking at what the uses of that water are that bring the most value to the community.” Agriculture has been a major part of Arizona’s economy since it became a state, and still gobbles up more than 70 percent of the state’s water. Industrial uses, including the chip manufacturing that’s had a foothold in the state since the 1940s, account for just 6 percent. While the amount of water that semiconductor factories, or fabs, use is still quite small compared to agriculture, the chip industry is growing fast. Fabs use “ultra-pure” water to clean surfaces and etch sensitive chips. It takes more municipal water to create a smaller amount of ultra-pure water through deionization and reverse osmosis. A typical facility might use 10 million gallons of ultra-pure water a day, which could require up to 16 million gallons of municipal water. New chip factories are sprouting up in Arizona’s desert with the help of federal funding. President Joe Biden signed the ​​CHIPS and Science Act into law in 2022, setting aside $52.7 billion to expand domestic chip manufacturing. Armed with a $7.86 billion grant from the government, Intel is planning to spend $32 billion on two new factories and an expansion of an existing facility in Arizona. In 2025, the company’s facilities in Chandler, Arizona withdrew more than 2.7 billion gallons of freshwater, according to its latest corporate responsibility report. TSMC, the world’s largest chipmaker, received up to $6.6 billion in CHIPS Act funding and decided to build at least six new semiconductor fabs in Phoenix. TSMC’s first fab in Arizona uses roughly 4.75 million gallons of water a day, the company told The Verge last year. It’s approximately equivalent to the water usage of more than 14,000 homes a day, or 2 percent of Phoenix’s housing. That amount grows with each new fab the company builds, and with the more advanced manufacturing processes TSMC is developing. The company recycles 65 percent of the water it uses in Arizona, TSMC says, a figure that’s supposed to grow to at least 90 percent when it finishes building a water reclamation plant. The Colorado River is the state’s biggest renewable source of water. But the Colorado River Basin has faced “unprecedented” drought for more than a quarter century, according to the US Bureau of Reclamation. Climate change, unfortunately, is also making the region more dry as growing water demand adds to decades of overuse. “There’s not enough water for everything we want to do with it,” Sorensen, who previously worked as the director of Phoenix Water Services, says. “So what do we have enough water for? What are the uses we most value? Is it cotton or is it microchips?” With 40 million Americans from Denver to Los Angeles relying on water from the Colorado River, states have been tussling over how to allocate the remaining water for years. Guidelines for how to manage that water, collectively known as the “Law of the River,” expire this year. After states failed to reach an agreement on their own, the US Department of the Interior finalized its own plan in August for how to move forward. It outlines steep cuts for downriver states: Arizona, Nevada, and California. Arizona stands to lose the most, at least 760,000 acre-feet of water a year starting in 2027. An acre-foot represents how much water it would take to cover an acre with a foot of water, and is enough to supply about three homes with water for a year in the Phoenix area. The City of Phoenix uses about 300,000 acre feet of water in a year. Maricopa County, home to Intel and TSMC’s chip fabs, isn’t as reliant on water from the Colorado River as other counties. Its primary resource is groundwater, but surface water flowing from the Colorado and Salt rivers still make up close to 40 percent of the county’s supply. Local leaders insist that Phoenix and other cities in the region are prepared for water cuts, citing plans to make up for the shortfall with underground water stores and other surface water sources. “For the most part, they’ve planned accordingly and can fall back onto water that was previously stored underground,” Sorensen says. But even without sudden tap water shortages, Sorensen expects utility bills to climb over time. The transition to alternative water resources will entail new infrastructure, like new wells and pipes. That’s likely to be the most significant driver of higher tap water prices, Sorensen explains. Meanwhile, the city of Phoenix is pushing back, with Mayor Kate Gallego arguing that the federal government’s decision to cut the state’s intake “does not provide the fair, basin-wide leadership the Colorado River crisis demands.” That said, “Phoenix is prepared for this moment because of decades of planning and conservation, we will push for new federal support to mitigate the rising cost of water that will result from this federal decision,” Gallego added in an August press release. A spokesperson for the city declined to comment further in an interview. TSMC in particular, located in Phoenix, will be subject to the same price hikes as its neighbors. Phoenix is unique in that it sets the same water rates for companies as it does for residential customers. Cities often charge industrial customers less if they want to attract certain businesses. “The cost of water will increase for TSMC,” Sorensen says. “Everyone pays the same rate for water in the city of Phoenix, whether you’re a mom-and-pop store, a family of eight, or TSMC.” TSMC and Intel declined interviews with The Verge for this story. Both have made public commitments, however, to minimize the amount of fresh water they consume. “A stable supply of water is critical to chip production,” TSMC deputy spokesperson Nina Kao said in an emailed statement. “One of the reasons the city of Phoenix was selected for our US expansion is because of their long-term water plan, which includes varied water supply sources, as well as steps taken in preparation for reduced water supplies over the course of decades.” Apprehensions are still mounting over the impact that AI and the tech industry as a whole have on the region. AI has spawned a new generation of semiconductor factories, chip packaging plants, and data centers across Arizona. “It’s almost happening at a level that’s difficult to wrap your head around,” says Jennifer Martin-McLeod, a program manager for the Grand Canyon chapter of Sierra Club. “To try to say ‘Everybody take a breath and think through what we’re doing’ is difficult when you have that steamroller of money coming at your state to try to make it all happen overnight.” She has broader concerns about the health of the Colorado River and wildlife that depends on it. Over the long term, Sorensen points out that a shortage of water from the Colorado River will result in the depletion of groundwater in Central Arizona, as most cities cope by increasing how much water they draw from local aquifers. “It’s something they can sustain, but it is only sustained at a cost to future generations,” she adds. The impact of water cuts next year will be felt most by typical residents, Martin-McLeod says. “For me, that’s going to mean serious lifestyle changes. … But to an enormous chip manufacturer, that’s maybe just part of the cost of doing business, you know?”

articles.title: Scientists fitted GPS collars to 17 lions and 14 hyenas expecting hyenas to follow lions; thousands of locations revealed the opposite, with male lions approaching as hyenas retreated
articles.summary: Wildlife & Biodiversity News: Wildlife biologists tracking lions and spotted hyenas in Southern Africa have found evidence that challenges a long-held belief about how the two pred.
articles.body: Wildlife biologists tracking lions and spotted hyenas in Southern Africa have found evidence that challenges a long-held belief about how the two predators interact. Instead of hyenas mainly following lions to find leftover food, the study found that male lions often actively move towards spotted hyenas, while the hyenas try to get away. The study, published in the open-access journal Frontiers in Ethology on September 9, 2026, used thousands of telemetry records to track the movements of the two species in real time. Researchers fitted high-precision GPS collars to 17 African lions (Panthera leo) and 14 spotted hyenas (Crocuta crocuta) living in protected wilderness areas. Researchers had initially expected hyena groups to regularly follow lions, either to take advantage of their kills or to scavenge food left behind. The tracking data showed a different pattern. Male lions often changed direction and moved towards nearby hyenas, while hyenas changed their routes or moved away to avoid potentially dangerous encounters.Tracking data reveals unexpected movement patternsThe international research team used location data collected at regular intervals across several seasons to study the movements of the predators. The large dataset allowed researchers to examine how lions and hyenas responded when they came close to one another, including at night and in areas that were difficult for researchers to observe directly. When male lions came close to spotted hyenas, their GPS tracks often showed a clear change in direction towards the hyenas. This indicated that the lions were not simply encountering their competitors by chance. Instead, they appeared to be actively moving towards them. The behaviour could help lions eliminate competitors or take over kills that hyenas had already secured. Lions and spotted hyenas compete for many of the same prey animals, making encounters between the two species potentially costly for both sides. The hyenas showed the opposite response. Their movement paths generally turned away when lions approached. They appeared to maintain a distance from male lions and changed direction or increased their speed when the predators came too close. "We expected hyenas to track lions to exploit their kills, but the GPS data clearly showed lions taking the initiative," noted the research team in their paper published in Frontiers in Ethology. "Male lions actively moved towards hyena locations, forcing hyenas to take evasive action to avoid dangerous confrontations." The researchers also found differences between male and female lions. Male lions were more likely to move towards hyenas, while lionesses showed more cautious movement. This was particularly noticeable when females were caring for dependent cubs or moving without the protection of a male coalition.The findings challenge the usual predator hierarchyThe results question a common picture of the relationship between lions and spotted hyenas. Spotted hyenas are skilled hunters and can kill large prey without relying on lions. Yet they are often portrayed as scavengers that follow big cats and steal their food. The relationship is more complicated. Lions can also take advantage of kills made by hyenas, particularly because adult male lions have a major physical advantage over individual female hyenas. Male lions can weigh up to twice as much as adult female hyenas. A single male can therefore drive several hyenas away from a carcass or seriously injure one during a confrontation. For hyenas, avoiding a direct fight can be the safer option unless enough members of the clan are present to challenge the lion. The tracking results suggest that this risk shapes where and how hyenas move when lions are nearby. The study therefore points to spatial avoidance as an important survival strategy for spotted hyenas living alongside lions. Hyenas can benefit from searching for food in areas used by lions, but they also have to manage the risk of coming too close to a much stronger predator.GPS collars offer a clearer view of predator behaviourMuch of what scientists previously knew about interactions between lions and hyenas came from observations made during research drives. Those observations can be limited because predators are not always active during daylight hours, while thick vegetation can prevent researchers from seeing encounters. GPS tracking provided a different view. The collars used in the study recorded the animals' locations at regular intervals, allowing researchers to follow their movements across day and night. The technology also made it possible to track animals through areas that researchers could not easily reach. By comparing the movements of lions and hyenas at the same time, scientists could see how one species responded when the other approached. The resulting data offered a more detailed picture of predator interactions than isolated sightings could provide. The research published in Frontiers in Ethology shows how multi-species tracking can help answer questions that have remained difficult to study through traditional field observations.Why the findings matter for wildlife reservesUnderstanding how large predators respond to one another can also help conservation managers plan for wildlife populations in protected areas. Human development has reduced and fragmented many natural habitats, leaving some predator populations increasingly concentrated inside protected reserves. In fenced reserves, lions, hyenas and other large carnivores may have less space to avoid one another or follow natural movement patterns. Knowing how predators respond when they share the same territory can help managers understand where different species are likely to concentrate and how their movements may affect prey populations. The researchers' findings suggest that the relationship between lions and hyenas cannot be described simply as hunters and scavengers. Their movements show a more active contest between two competing predators, with male lions often taking the initiative and spotted hyenas adjusting their behaviour to stay out of danger.

articles.title: Where Did Canada’s Last 6 Captive Belugas Go?
articles.summary: Canada just completed what experts call the largest captive whale relocation in history, and the journey these six belugas took to reach their new homes was...
articles.body:
Canada's last six captive beluga whales were relocated from Marineland to new homes, marking the end of whale or dolphin captivity in the country.

The whales were carefully guided into transport slings, lifted with a crane, and flown to their new homes after the closure of Marineland.

The relocation of the beluga whales was described as the largest ever undertaken, with two going to Shedd Aquarium in Chicago and four to SeaWorld in San Antonio.

Whales are some of nature's most amazing animals. Growing to massive sizes, these animals deserve to spend their time traveling the open seas. Recently, Canada's last captive whales were relocated from the former Marineland to new homes. This Instagram post by @walrus_whisperer shows the parade of vehicles carrying these whales.

On August 31, the final six beluga whales began their removal from the now-shuttered Marineland marine park in Niagara Falls, Canada. This has been described as the largest relocation of captive whales ever undertaken. The whales lived at Marineland, which was once Canada's best-known marine attraction. The park closed to the public in 2024, leaving 30 beluga whales and four bottlenose dolphins behind. As the facility faced growing financial problems and prepared to sell the property, the urgency of finding new homes for the animals increased. Thanks to collaboration between Canadian authorities, veterinarians, and transport crews, the final six whales at the facility were ultimately relocated to new homes.

Two of the whales, Yukon and Gimli, were sent to Shedd Aquarium in Chicago, while Tank, Odin, Orion, and Tofino were sent to SeaWorld in San Antonio. The other beluga whales and dolphins have been distributed to several different facilities in Atlanta, San Diego, and Valencia, Spain. Moving animals of this size requires careful planning. Specialists carefully guided each beluga whale into a transport sling, which was then lifted with a crane.

They were lowered into water-filled transport tanks and then brought to Toronto Pearson International Airport, from where they were flown to their new homes. Traveling is extremely stressful for any animal, but it can be especially difficult for social animals like whales. Because transport can be stressful, veterinarians monitored the whales closely before, during, and after the journey. This move is extremely significant as it marks the end of whale or dolphin captivity in Canada.

articles.title: Lessons from Ukraine war: Poland wants its own Starlink; where does India stand?
articles.summary: News News: Poland is moving to develop its own military satellite communications system in partnership with Finnish space company ICEYE and state-run defence gia.
articles.body: Poland is moving to develop its own military satellite communications system in partnership with Finnish space company ICEYE and state-run defence giant PGZ, in a programme that Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk described as a potential “Polish Starlink”.The two companies signed a letter of intent for the project at the MSPO defence show in Kielce on Sept. 9. Tusk said the planned system would be modelled on SpaceX’s Starlink satellite network, highlighting the critical role of communications in modern warfare.Under the new partnership, ICEYE will serve as the technology partner, developing the satellite architecture, manufacturing the spacecraft and conducting satellite operations, while PGZ will establish the domestic industrial base and coordinate Polish companies contributing production capabilities, expertise and infrastructure.According to Defense News, PGZ said the programme is planned for implementation between 2026 and 2030. The system is expected to use a distributed satellite architecture, alongside domestic ground infrastructure and industrial capabilities that would allow Poland to independently develop and maintain the system.“Anyone closely following the Russian-Ukrainian war knows how important communications are,” Tusk said, adding that communications are “absolutely critical” on the modern battlefield.Starlink's role in the Ukraine warThe Ukraine war has demonstrated the military value of satellite communications, with SpaceX’s Starlink becoming an important communications network for Ukrainian forces.According to Reuters, Ukrainian military units were heavily reliant on thousands of Starlink terminals for battlefield communications and some drone operations, with the systems proving resistant to espionage and signal jamming.The dependence on Starlink has also exposed the risks of relying on a privately operated system during a war. In July 2025, a global Starlink outage disrupted Ukrainian military communications for about two and a half hours, affecting drone operations and battlefield coordination. A Ukrainian drone commander said several combat operations had to be postponed during the outage.European governments have increasingly looked at reducing their dependence on US satellite communications infrastructure, with the war highlighting both the value of Starlink and the vulnerabilities that can arise from reliance on a single provider.Where India standsIndia has dedicated military satellite communications capabilities for more than a decade. The Indian Navy was the first service to receive a dedicated communications satellite with GSAT-7, launched in 2013. The Indian Air Force later received GSAT-7A, launched in 2018, which provides communication capability to users over the Indian region.A recent assessment by Germany's Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik notes that the GSAT series has increasingly been used to meet India's military communications requirements, with GSAT-7 providing the Navy's sovereign communications infrastructure and GSAT-7A extending such capability to the other armed forces.India has now added a newer and more capable layer to this architecture. CMS-03, also designated GSAT-7R, was launched on November 2, 2025, and was developed specifically for the Indian Navy. The government describes it as India's most advanced communication satellite for the Navy, designed to strengthen space-based communications and maritime domain awareness. The satellite provides coverage across the Indian Ocean Region and weighs about 4,400 kg, making it India's heaviest communication satellite launched from Indian soil.The CMS-03 satellite is intended to support naval communications across a very large maritime area, giving the Navy a dedicated space-based communications layer for operations across the Indian Ocean.

articles.title: Archaeopteryx: Como a primeira ave decolava há 150 milhões de anos | G1
articles.standfirst: Um ícone da evolução, o Archaeopteryx é a ramificação mais antiga na linhagem das aves que conhecemos, mas mesmo sem as adaptações dos pássaros modernos já era eficiente na sua “decolagem”
articles.summary: Estudo sobre o Archaeopteryx revela que a primeira ave usava saltos para decolar, desvendando um mistério da evolução das aves e do voo dos dinossauros.
articles.body:
Archaeopteryx: estudo revela como a ‘primeira ave’ levantava voo há 150 milhões de anos — Foto: Adobe Stock

O Archaeopteryx é um ícone da evolução e costuma ser chamado de a “primeira ave”. Os cientistas há muito debatem como exatamente ele decolava do solo, mas um estudo recente publicado por mim e meus colegas trouxe novas perspectivas para esse mistério.

Nosso estudo comparou o Archaeopteryx com a anatomia das aves modernas, e nossas descobertas sugerem que ele gerava a força necessária para decolar dando vários saltos para a frente.

O Archaeopteryx , um fóssil descoberto em rochas jurássicas da Alemanha, remonta a 150 milhões de anos. Ele era coberto de penas e tinha asas , mas mantinha uma série de características distintivas dos dinossauros, como uma longa cauda óssea , garras em dedos separados e dentes em uma mandíbula sem bico.

Charles Darwin previu, na primeira edição de A Origem das Espécies , publicada em 1859, que mais tarde seriam encontrados fósseis ligando os principais grupos de animais. Um ano após a publicação, uma pena, e, em menos de dois anos, um esqueleto completo de Archaeopteryx foram descobertos, mostrando ligações claras entre as aves e os dinossauros. O Archaeopteryx é uma dessas formas de transição que ligam um grupo a outro.

O “primeiro pássaro” não estava perfeitamente desenvolvido como as aves que evoluíram até hoje. Mas não seria de se esperar que estivesse. Ele tinham músculos de voo relativamente fracos, sem esterno com quilha para uma fixação muscular forte, e não poderia ter levantado as asas acima da horizontal.

Em vez de chamá-lo de primeiro pássaro, é melhor descrevê-lo como a espécie de ramificação mais antiga, até onde se sabe, na linhagem das aves, após todo o grupo das aves ter se separado dos dinossauros não avianos há mais de 150 milhões de anos.

Em 2016, meu amigo Colin Palmer convidou um colega, Markus Heller (professor de biomecânica), e a mim para nos juntarmos a ele na exploração de um problema complexo: como as primeiras aves se libertaram das amarras da Terra e levantaram voo?

Palmer vinha trabalhando há mais de uma década com os primos voadores dos dinossauros, os pterossauros, e também com um dinossauro peculiar (embora agora seja um entre vários conhecidos) de quatro asas, emplumado e voador chamado Microraptor . Os pterossauros, no entanto, não são dinossauros, e o Microraptor é um dinossauro mais próximo do Velociraptor (pequenos dinossauros carnívoros) do que das aves.

Uma série de mecanismos foram sugeridos para a evolução do voo e da decolagem. Literalmente, do chão para cima, ou das árvores para baixo, até bater as asas enquanto se corre para subir uma ladeira. O problema é que isso é difícil de testar experimentalmente. Por isso, recorremos ao melhor exemplo de decolagem que existe: o das próprias aves.

Palmer já havia filmado várias aves por curiosidade. Assim como outros cientistas já tinham observado, mas nunca aprofundado, Palmer percebeu que todas elas exibiam o mesmo tipo de comportamento antes da decolagem: pular com as duas patas. As asas pareciam ter pouca participação na decolagem da ave, e isso abriu algumas possibilidades para a pesquisa sobre as aves mais primitivas.

Os ancestrais das aves, os dinossauros terópodes, tinham patas poderosas . Eles definitivamente podiam pular, e pular poderia proporcionar uma importante vantagem evolutiva. Ser capaz de se esquivar de um predador, e talvez dar uma batida com as asas emplumadas para prolongar o salto, poderia muito bem salvar sua vida.

A primeira parte dessa pesquisa, que realizamos com o então estudante de graduação Erik Meilak, consistiu em desenvolver um método para verificar quanta força os membros posteriores das aves geram ao decolar do solo. Utilizamos uma placa de força (uma balança de cozinha modificada) e um computador Raspberry Pi para controlar a fotografia em alta velocidade, juntamente com tomografia computadorizada do esqueleto para observar exatamente como os ossos se articulavam. Descobrimos como as pegas - uma ave da família dos corvos- decolavam. Elas usavam as pernas como principal fonte de força.

Esse projeto de verão na graduação de Meilak se tornou um projeto de doutorado completo, com ele analisando várias outras espécies de aves, como estorninhos e corvos. Trabalhamos com a bióloga evolutiva Pauline Provini, em Paris, que tinha realizado pesquisas com pombas e tentilhões, demonstrando como todas essas aves usavam as pernas na decolagem.

Com a cinemática detalhada — todas as forças e momentos gerados pelos músculos ao redor das articulações dos membros posteriores —, adaptamos o modelo ao Archaeopteryx e verificamos se o primeiro pássaro poderia levantar voo de maneira semelhante às aves modernas.

O Archaeopteryx está, por definição, 150 milhões de anos atrás dos “saltos” das aves modernas e não poderia decolar como as observamos fazerem quando assustadas: de forma explosiva, com um único salto, para depois começar a bater as asas rumo ao céu. O Archaeopteryx não poderia fazer isso e, como disse, não podia contar com suas asas para batidas poderosas.

Por isso, nos perguntamos “o que suas pernas poderiam fazer?”. E, assim como as aves de hoje, ao decolar de forma mais tranquila, demonstramos que o Archaeopteryx já poderia ter levantado voo com dois saltos com as pernas . Ele também poderia usar três saltos, aumentando a velocidade e, uma vez no ar, suas asas batendo manteriam uma velocidade de voo de 7 metros por segundo.

O Archaeopteryx também poderia acrescentar um batimento de asas - salto-batida-salto - para atingir essa velocidade com apenas dois saltos. Tudo isso sem a anatomia altamente evoluída e adaptada ao voo de pombos, corvos, gaviões e até mesmo galinhas.

No futuro, talvez encontremos um fóssil que ainda seja uma ave em vez de um dinossauro não aviano, mas que seja menos, digamos, “aviano” do que o Archaeopteryx , e então esse se tornaria o táxon mais antigo do ramo. Mas ainda não encontramos. Portanto, o Archaeopteryx permanece em seu lugar como a primeira ave que conhecemos.

Neil J. Gostling é professor associado da Faculdade de Ciências Biológicas da Universidade de Southampton. O trabalho aqui descrito foi financiado pelo Conselho de Pesquisa do Meio Ambiente Natural (número da concessão NE/L002531/1).

articles.title: Exploran las profundidades del océano y encuentran 1.121 especies desconocidas: algunas parecen de otro planeta
articles.standfirst: El Ocean Census identifica más de un millar de nuevas especies marinas en zonas del océano de hasta 6.575 metros de profundidad
articles.summary: El Ocean Census identifica más de un millar de nuevas especies marinas en zonas del océano de hasta 6.575 metros de profundidad
articles.body: Explorar las profundidades del océano sigue sacando a la luz formas de vida que hasta ahora eran desconocidas para la ciencia. Durante el último año, un equipo internacional de investigadores ha identificado 1.121 nuevas especies marinas, algunas recogidas a miles de metros bajo la superficie y con características que parecen sacadas de otro mundo. Los hallazgos forman parte del tercer año de trabajo del Ocean Census, una iniciativa internacional impulsada por The Nippon Foundation y Nekton que busca acelerar la identificación y catalogación de especies marinas. En esta última campaña participaron científicos de distintas instituciones en 13 expediciones y nueve talleres especializados para analizar las muestras obtenidas en algunas de las regiones oceánicas menos exploradas. Las especies fueron encontradas en diferentes ecosistemas marinos y a profundidades de hasta 6.575 metros. Entre ellas hay peces, crustáceos, corales, anémonas, erizos de mar y otros invertebrados. El proyecto destaca que algunas de estas zonas siguen siendo prácticamente desconocidas debido a las enormes dificultades que existen para acceder a ellas. El volumen del hallazgo también resulta llamativo. Según Ocean Census, las 1.121 especies identificadas suponen un aumento del 54% en el ritmo anual de identificación de especies marinas respecto a la situación anterior. Entre los descubrimientos hay especies especialmente llamativas. Los investigadores identificaron una nueva especie de quimera, conocida popularmente como tiburón fantasma, en el mar del Coral. Estos animales son parientes lejanos de los tiburones y las rayas y viven en aguas profundas. También encontraron un peculiar gusano de cerdas asociado a estructuras volcánicas submarinas en Japón. El animal mantiene una relación simbiótica con otros organismos y fue localizado en un entorno que los investigadores describen como un "castillo de cristal". La lista incluye además nuevas especies de corales, cangrejos, camarones, erizos de mar y anémonas. No todas presentan un aspecto extraordinario, pero el hecho de que hayan permanecido fuera de los registros científicos muestra hasta qué punto continúa sin conocerse buena parte de la biodiversidad marina. El Ocean Census calcula que más del 90% de las especies del océano todavía podrían no haber sido descubiertas, aunque esta cifra es una estimación sobre la biodiversidad marina que aún no ha sido catalogada y no significa que exista un porcentaje concreto de especies que los científicos sepan que están ahí sin haberlas visto. La iniciativa intenta además reducir el tiempo que transcurre entre el descubrimiento de un organismo y su incorporación formal al conocimiento científico. Históricamente, Ocean Census señala que el intervalo medio entre encontrar una especie y describirla científicamente ha sido de 13,5 años. Su nueva plataforma, NOVA, pretende poner los datos de nuevas especies a disposición de investigadores mucho antes, en algunos casos en cuestión de días o semanas. Los científicos siguen ampliando esta búsqueda. De hecho, el programa continúa realizando expediciones y talleres en 2026, incluida una nueva investigación sobre posibles especies desconocidas en el Atlántico Sur y el océano Austral. El objetivo es acelerar el conocimiento de unos ecosistemas que, pese a cubrir la mayor parte del planeta, siguen escondiendo una cantidad extraordinaria de vida.

articles.title: Around AD 310, a Roman emperor had a private bath built with three pools, heated floors and a sauna; archaeologists have now uncovered its unusual design
articles.summary: Archaeology & Ancient World News: Nearly 1,700 years ago, an emperor could retreat from the demands of the Roman court without leaving his palace. Beneath a monumental tower in what is.
articles.body: Nearly 1,700 years ago, an emperor could retreat from the demands of the Roman court without leaving his palace. Beneath a monumental tower in what is now eastern Serbia, he had a private bathing suite built with heated floors, multiple pools and a sauna — a remarkably sophisticated space designed for comfort, privacy and relaxation. Archaeologists have now uncovered the remains of that unusual bath complex, offering a glimpse into the luxurious lifestyle of Roman Emperor Maximinus Daza and the engineering behind his imperial residence.A palace built for an emperorThe discovery was made at Vrelo-Šarkamen, a fortified residential complex constructed in the early fourth century. The site is associated with Maximinus Daza, who ruled as Roman emperor from 310 to 313. Excavations at the site have continued intermittently for decades, but recent work by researchers from Serbia’s Institute of Archaeology has revealed that the palace was considerably more elaborate than previously understood.Maximinus Daza, whose full name was Galerius Valerius Maximinus, was born in the region and rose to power during one of the most turbulent periods of the Roman Empire. He was part of the tetrarchy, a system established by Emperor Diocletian in which the vast empire was governed by four rulers. The arrangement was already beginning to unravel by the time Maximinus became emperor. His reign lasted only a few years, ending with his defeat by his rival Licinius and his death in 313.A bath unlike the usual Roman modelThe most intriguing discovery lies beneath a monumental tower at the southwest corner of the palace. Rather than following the more familiar linear arrangement found in many Roman bathhouses, with rooms placed one after another, this private bath was circular and occupied the lowest level of the tower. Its unusual layout appears to have been carefully adapted to the architecture of the building. The room was covered by a dome fitted with six windows, an architectural feature that would have required considerable technical skill. The design also allowed the bath to combine practical infrastructure with an enclosed space intended for the emperor and other members of the palace elite.Heated floors and three bathing poolsThe bath, known in Latin as a balneum, was divided into two main areas. One section housed the equipment needed to keep the complex running. Archaeologists found the remains of a furnace that would have heated the floors, a hallmark of Roman bathing technology. They also uncovered the base of a copper boiler used to heat water, although the boiler itself has disappeared. The second section was devoted to bathing and relaxation. Inside, researchers found three bathing pools or tubs, along with a sudatorium, a room designed for steam bathing or sauna-like relaxation. Together, the features point to a space that was about far more than basic hygiene.A glimpse into imperial lifeFor the Roman elite, bathing could be an important part of daily life, combining relaxation, socialising and personal care. In this case, however, the setting suggests something more private and exclusive. The bath was incorporated directly into the emperor’s palace, with its heating system, bathing areas and sophisticated architecture working together within a relatively compact space. Its position inside the tower also raises questions about how Maximinus Daza and his family reached the complex.Archaeologists plan to continue investigating the site, hoping to reconstruct the arrangement of the rooms and understand how the bath functioned within the wider palace.What survives at Vrelo-Šarkamen is more than a collection of ancient walls. It is a snapshot of imperial life at a moment when the Roman world was changing rapidly — preserved beneath a tower where an emperor once had the luxury of disappearing into his own private bath.Images Courtesy: Vrelo-Šarkamen research team/Institute of Archaeology

articles.title: Former NASA specialist claims he has found a way to overcome Earth's gravity in a 'major discovery'
articles.summary: Space & Astronomy News: A former NASA engineer claims he has found a way to overcome Earth's gravity, and all ears have perked up. Exodus Propulsion Technologies, a private c.
articles.body: A former NASA engineer claims he has found a way to overcome Earth's gravity, and all ears have perked up. Exodus Propulsion Technologies, a private company co-founded by Charles Buhler, an electrostatics specialist has made the claim, according to a report by Popular Mechanics. With Buhler having worked for NASA and Kennedy Space Centre, his words have made for an extremely interesting pedigree.Previously, Buhler has helped establish the Electrostatics and Surface Physics Laboratory at Kennedy Space Centre in Florida, a very important lab that ensures rockets don't explode. He is a veteran of storied programs such as NASA’s Space Shuttle, the International Space Station (ISS), The Hubble Telescope, and the current NASA Dust Program. Now, with his own company, he has argued that his team has found a propellantless effect driven by electric fields, a 'New Force' that can generate enough thrust to counter gravity, as he described it to The Debrief.“The most important message to convey to the public is that a major discovery occurred,” Buhler told The Debrief. “This discovery of a New Force is fundamental in that electric fields alone can generate a sustainable force onto an object and allow centre-of-mass translation of said object without expelling mass.”In an interview with APEC’s co-founder Tim Ventura, Buhler explained how his background in electrostatics led to the discovery. He says his team, made up of people from NASA, Blue Origin, and the Air Force, investigated propellant-less drives for two decades before arriving at electrostatics. “Nature has its own way of doing things,” Buhler explained, “and it is our job to uncover what nature does. It just happened to fall into my lap in what I’m the expert in.”For years, their devices produced negligible thrust, but saw increases with each new iteration. For example, from 2016 to the end of 2020, their best devices were producing a little more than one hundred thousandth of a gravity. In the coming years, that would go up exponentially. For clarification, Buhler said that measuring thrust in terms of a percentage of gravity reflects the force generated divided by the test article.“The aim is to approach and exceed unity,” he explained, “which means the article would generate enough thrust to lift itself in Earth’s gravity, and that’s defined as 1 gravity of thrust.”Buhler says they commonly measured the forces in milliNewtons, but they prefer to describe the thrust in terms of gravity since that is the ultimate goal of propulsion physics. “The highest we have generated on a stacked system is about 10 mN,” he said. “The magnitude is not important, really, since anything above zero would work in space!”In the years and months leading up to the breakthrough thrust measurement, Buhler and his team took great care to methodically eliminate anything else that could account for the tiny yet measurable force they were seeing. This detailed and painstaking work resulted in the team’s overriding patent, which was granted in 2020.With fresh momentum, Buhler says they also began construction of a custom-made vacuum chamber that would allow them to simulate the environment of deep space. If something else was causing the force, this chamber was built to identify it.According to the APEC presentation, that chamber was completed at the end of 2020. Between January and September 2021, 146 separate articles were tested, each seemingly confirming the presence of measurable thrust. The team also tested different configurations that eliminated the old designs using asymmetrical capacitors and instead employed models with opposing asymmetrical plates.Then, in 2022, something astounding happened. According to Buhler, his team began to see significant jumps in the force being generated. A quick look at a chart he presented to APEC shows that tests performed between early 2022 and November 2023 resulted in a rapid climb, moving from one thousandth, one hundredth, and even one-tenth of gravity all the way up to one full Earth gravity. This means that their current devices, which Buhler told “weigh somewhere between 30-40 grams on their own” without the attached test equipment, were producing enough thrust to counteract the full force of one Earth gravity. This culminated in 2023, when this “New Force”-powered drive generated enough thrust to overcome Earth’s gravity.After decades of research, Buhler says he and his team had shown unequivocally that a new, fundamental force was at work and that his devices were tapping into that force to produce thrust without emitting any mass or propellant.“Essentially, what we’ve discovered is that systems that contain an asymmetry in either electrostatic pressure or some kind of electrostatic divergent field can give a system of a centre of mass a non-zero force component,” Buhler explained. “So, what that basically means is that there’s some underlying physics that can essentially place force on an object should those two constraints be met.”APEC event listings in January, March, and May 2026 described continued “testing and refinement” by Exodus co-founder Andrew Aurigema. In a March 2026 interview, Buhler said he had run roughly 2,000 vacuum-chamber experiments and was emphasising effects such as thrust that allegedly persisted after power was turned off.Buhler stressed that this work is unaffiliated with NASA. Much of the public discussion has moved through the Alternative Propulsion Energy Conference, or APEC, a community built around advanced-propulsion ideas that range from serious engineering questions to claims that still need far more careful testing.Exodus has also moved into a more openly investor-facing phase. An official Deep Tech Week NYC 2026 listing advertised an “Exodus Propulsion Technologies - Meet and Greet” on April 4, inviting physicists and investors to discuss the technology and meet Buhler as CEO/founder.As of May 2026, there isn’t a published independent replication using an outside lab’s own apparatus, instrumentation, and uncertainty budget.Previously, in 2001, British Electrical Engineer Roger Shawyer first introduced the “impossible drive,” known as the EmDrive. It earned that nickname because Shawyer claimed it could produce thrust without propellant. The EmDrive spent years producing tantalising little signals, including a reported thrust measurement from NASA’s Eagleworks team in 2016. Then better tests caught up. By 2021, work at the Dresden University of Technology found no thrust from the device, turning one of the most famous propellantless-drive claims into a cautionary tale about tiny forces, experimental noise, and wishful machinery.Up next, Buhler says his team is seeking funding to test their devices in space to better understand the force at work.“We’re hoping to do some demos,” said Buhler. “Some space demos. That’s what we’re trying to get some funding to do. I think that would be a great way to show off the technology.”

articles.title: For decades, scientists thought North America had its own cheetah; ancient DNA reveals the extinct cat split from the puma lineage 2.6 million years ago
articles.summary: Wildlife & Biodiversity News: Its appearance told one story; its DNA tells another. For decades, the extinct Miracinonyx trumani was known as the “American cheetah” because its lon.
articles.body: Its appearance told one story; its DNA tells another. For decades, the extinct Miracinonyx trumani was known as the “American cheetah” because its long legs, slender body and adaptations for speed made it look remarkably similar to Africa’s modern cheetahs. But a new genetic study has overturned that long-held picture. Published in Current Biology, the research used ancient DNA from fossil remains to show that M. trumani was actually a close relative of the modern puma, with the two lineages diverging about 2.6 million years ago. The study also reveals that some of these supposedly cheetah-like cats had a surprising diet, with northern populations apparently eating fish in the Arctic.The “American cheetah” was not actually a cheetahMiracinonyx trumani lived across parts of North America during the Pleistocene, with evidence placing the species from roughly 2.5 million to 16,000 years ago. Fossils showed that it had a body built for running, including long limbs and a relatively slender frame. Those characteristics led scientists to compare it with the modern cheetah, and the nickname “American cheetah” became widely used. The new genetic evidence, however, tells a different evolutionary story.Researchers analysed nuclear DNA from four M. trumani fossils, including specimens from Wyoming and the Yukon in northwestern Canada. By comparing their genomes with those of living and extinct cats, they found that M. trumani was a sister species of the modern puma, rather than a close relative of the cheetah. The two lineages separated roughly 2.6 million years ago. That means the similarities between the extinct cat and today's cheetahs were not evidence of close ancestry. Instead, they were an example of convergent evolution, in which unrelated animals independently develop similar physical characteristics because they face similar environmental pressures.Why did it look so much like a cheetah?The resemblance makes sense when the animal's lifestyle is considered. Both M. trumani and modern cheetahs evolved body shapes suited to fast movement. Long limbs and a lightweight build would have helped M. trumani pursue prey across open landscapes. But appearance can sometimes give scientists an incomplete picture of an extinct animal. Without genetic evidence, it was difficult to determine whether the American cat had inherited its body shape from a cheetah-like ancestor or had independently evolved similar features. The DNA has now provided a clearer answer.According to the researchers, the name “American cheetah” can therefore be misleading because it suggests both a close genetic relationship and a specialised hunting lifestyle similar to that of modern cheetahs. Neither assumption is supported by the new evidence.Ancient DNA reveals a surprising Arctic dietThe genetic discovery was not the only surprise. The researchers also examined stable carbon and nitrogen isotopes preserved in the fossils to reconstruct what the animals ate. The results suggested that M. trumani was not necessarily a specialised hunter of terrestrial herbivores throughout its range. The northern specimens, recovered from the Yukon, showed chemical signatures consistent with a diet rich in aquatic animals. Researchers believe these cats may have eaten fish, potentially including salmon.They may have caught fish themselves, scavenged fish after spawning or used both strategies. The available evidence cannot determine exactly how the animals obtained their aquatic food. That finding is particularly striking because the northern M. trumani populations lived in an environment very different from the grasslands where their southern counterparts hunted. The Wyoming specimen, by comparison, had isotope signatures more consistent with a predator feeding largely on terrestrial herbivores. This suggests that the species could adjust its diet substantially depending on where it lived.The cat's range was larger than scientists realisedThe Yukon fossils also expand the known geographical range of M. trumani by about 20 degrees of latitude farther north than previously recognised. The findings indicate that the species was capable of surviving in remarkably different environments, from temperate parts of North America to the Arctic. Researchers say this flexibility resembles the adaptability seen in modern pumas, which occupy a wide range of habitats and consume many types of prey.Genetic evidence also revealed changes that may have helped northern populations cope with extreme seasonal light conditions. Researchers identified loss-of-function mutations in genes involved in regulating circadian rhythms, potentially reflecting adaptation to the very long periods of daylight and darkness found at high latitudes.Why did the American cheetah disappear?The study also offers clues about the species' eventual extinction. Researchers found that M. trumani had relatively low genetic diversity in both the Wyoming and Yukon populations. However, the animals did not show the signs of severe inbreeding or sudden population collapse that scientists might expect immediately before extinction. Instead, their genetic diversity appears to have declined gradually over a long period. The researchers suggest that this slow loss may have reduced the species' ability to respond to environmental changes, potentially contributing to its eventual extinction. M. trumani eventually disappeared around 16,000 years ago, during the later stages of the last Ice Age.The discovery ultimately changes more than the family tree of one extinct predator. It shows how much scientists can miss when an ancient animal is reconstructed mainly from its bones and appearance. The so-called American cheetah may have looked like a speed specialist, but its DNA and diet reveal something more complex: an adaptable North American cat that was genetically closer to today's pumas and capable of surviving in environments ranging from temperate grasslands to the Arctic.

articles.title: Scientists built a system that watches activity across nearly every cell of a living vertebrate at once; transparent zebrafish revealed body-wide signals moving between organs
articles.summary: Experiments & Discoveries News: The body is never truly quiet. Even when an animal appears to be resting, billions of cells are sending signals, responding to changes and coordinatin.
articles.body: The body is never truly quiet. Even when an animal appears to be resting, billions of cells are sending signals, responding to changes and coordinating with organs far beyond their immediate surroundings. For scientists, the challenge has always been hearing enough of that conversation at once. Researchers at HHMI’s Janelia Research Campus have now developed a system called WHOLISTIC, short for Whole Organism Live Imaging System for recording Tissue and IntraCellular activity. Published in the journal called Nature, the report states that the technology can capture real-time cellular activity across nearly the entire body of a living vertebrate, offering an unusually broad view of how organs and cells work together.Using transparent larval zebrafish, the team observed activity across systems including the brain, muscles, cardiovascular system and digestive organs simultaneously as the animals moved, ate and rested.From individual cells to the whole animalThe work was developed by Virginie Ruetten, a postdoctoral researcher in Misha Ahrens’ Janelia lab, along with collaborators at University College London, Virginia Tech and Tsinghua University. The key for the study was calcium. Nearly every cell uses changes in calcium levels to communicate and coordinate activity. By making these changes visible, researchers could follow the signals passing through different parts of the body.The Ahrens lab had previously developed techniques for recording calcium activity throughout the brain of larval zebrafish. WHOLISTIC takes that idea much further by extending the view beyond the brain and into the rest of the animal. The researchers first introduced a calcium sensor into cells throughout the fish. They then used specialized microscopy to capture the signals, developed computational tools to align and interpret the enormous amount of data, and used whole-body expansion microscopy to examine the animals at much higher resolution. The result is a system that can move between two scales that are normally studied separately: individual cells and the entire organism.According to the study, this gap has long limited researchers’ ability to understand how different biological systems interact. Ruetten describes the approach as a way to bridge those two fundamental scales of biology and fill an observability gap that has made cellular responses difficult to study at such scale.The body is more connected than it looksWHOLISTIC has already revealed patterns that might be missed when scientists examine organs individually. Researchers found widespread correlations between activity in the brain, muscles and internal organs. They also discovered that many cell types have distinctive patterns of activity over time, potentially allowing scientists to identify cells based on their behavior even when they lack specific labels.One particularly striking finding emerged when the fish experienced low-oxygen conditions. The researchers observed a body-wide response in which the brainstem helped redirect blood flow away from the gut and toward the brain and muscles, revealing how several systems cooperate to help the animal survive.The technology also uncovered waves of activity traveling along the spinal cord and brain during extended periods of motor inactivity. These signals originated in ependymal cells, which line the fluid-filled spaces of the central nervous system, raising the possibility that these cells have a role in sleep.Other experiments identified cells that respond to cold, including chondrocytes, the cells that make up cartilage, and showed that ketamine activates not only neurons but also cells and connective tissue surrounding the brain.A wider view of behaviorThe researchers are now adapting WHOLISTIC for Danionella, a tiny fish that remains transparent throughout its life. Unlike larval zebrafish, Danionella can therefore provide a window into more developed animals and more complex behaviors. Ahrens sees the broader approach as a way to rethink how scientists study biological systems. Looking only at the brain to understand behavior, he says, is similar to trying to understand a large corporation by examining only one department. The important clues may lie in the flow of information between different parts of the organization. For now, WHOLISTIC is still a long way from providing a complete picture of an entire human body. But by allowing researchers to watch cells, organs and behavior unfold together, the technique offers something biology has rarely had: a chance to see the pieces of a living system communicating in real time.Images Courtesy: istock and Nature

articles.title: The universe’s beautiful fine-tuning leaves atheism facing its biggest question
articles.summary: A Getty Museum visit with Leonardo da Vinci's art sparked a former atheist's journey into the anthropic principle and our fine-tuned universe.
articles.body: Years ago, at Los Angeles’ Getty Museum, I was given the rare privilege of a personal, after-hours tour of Leonardo da Vinci’s artwork. Standing alone in the quiet, dimly lit gallery, mere inches from a sepia-colored sketch of a human face composed of several dozen perfectly placed wavy lines, I knew without a doubt I was in the presence of pure genius. After years of being an atheist for whom science was god and the cosmos was a miraculous accident, I now know with equal certainty our universe, too, is a work of pure genius. Why is that? 'MILESTONE': SCIENTISTS CLAIM TO BUILD SYNTHETIC CELL, RAISING CONCERNS IN STEP TOWARD ARTIFICIAL LIFE In 1973, scientists from around the world gathered in Kraków, Poland, to celebrate the 500th birthday of Nicolaus Copernicus. Part of the conference concerned a 50-year-old unsolved mystery called the "large-number coincidences." The numerical values of natural phenomena large and small – the radius of the observable universe, the charge of an electron, the strength of gravity and so forth – follow a pattern hard to dismiss as mere coincidence. What could possibly explain this? METEORITE THAT CRASHED INTO NJ HOME HOLDS BUILDING BLOCKS OF LIFE, SCIENTISTS SAY Australian physicist Brandon Carter stood before the August gathering and offered a provocative observation that came to be called the Anthropic Principle. The special numerical "coincidences," he said, are inexorably linked to the one thing that makes our universe special: we and our fellow lifeforms. Without life, the universe would be an unremarkable ghost town. Carter’s presentation ignited the explosive birth of a brand-new science dedicated to fully answering the 50-year-old mystery: Is it mere coincidence our universe has just the right numerical composition for life to be possible — especially life as complex as humans — or is there more to it than that? SCIENTISTS REVIVE ANCIENT 24,000-YEAR-OLD ‘ZOMBIE WORM’ FROM ARCTIC ICE — THEN IT REPRODUCED Think of when you get your annual physical. The nurse measures your four core vital signs — body temperature, blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate — which yield a pattern of numbers that reveals important information about your insides. The universe’s numerical profile serves the same purpose: it tells us something essential about the inner being of the cosmos. And what it tells us, after decades of careful examination involving increasingly precise astronomical observations, laboratory experiments and theoretical calculations, is that our universe is not merely a coincidence. Far from it. "I find it quite improbable that such order came out of chaos," stated the late American cosmologist and former atheist Allan Sandage. "There has to be some organizing principle." COULD NOAH'S ARK REMAINS BE BURIED IN TURKEY? NEW FINDINGS REVIVE AGE-OLD DEBATE British astronomer Sir Fred Hoyle, whom I had the honor of getting to know as a grad student at Cornell, concurred: "A commonsense interpretation of the facts suggests that a super-intellect has monkeyed with physics… and that there are no blind forces worth speaking about in nature. The numbers one calculates from the facts seem to me so overwhelming as to put this conclusion almost beyond question." This startling revelation does not set well with atheists, who twist themselves into knots trying to defend the belief that everything — life and all — is but a happy accident, courtesy of purposeless laws of nature. The problem they have is explaining where those supposedly blind natural agents came from. Another valiant attempt to rescue the naturalistic worldview is the multiverse hypothesis. If there are an infinite number of universes, then it is no surprise at least one of them — ours — is tailor-made for life. But many decades of seeking ways to test this fantastic idea have failed. That’s because parallel universes are in principle isolated from one another and therefore beyond the reach of our observations. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION "The idea that we live in a multiverse is a fringe idea in a small part of a subfield of the physics community," says German theoretical physicist Sabine Hossenfelder. "Nobody who does serious science works with the multiverse because it’s utterly useless." So, then, we all now face this burning question screaming for an answer: If our universe is not a coincidence, how do we explain it? AMERICA ISN’T DONE WITH JESUS — AND THE BESTSELLER LIST JUST PROVED IT For me, the answer goes back to that unforgettable day at the Getty. As I stood there, seized by the ineffable beauty of Leonardo da Vinci’s exquisite sketch, it never would have occurred to me to entertain the notion that it was an accident.
